mcqs.question: A parent process needs to know when one of its background children exits so it can reap it. Which signal tells it?
options: SIGCHLD
SIGCONT
SIGTERM
SIGINT
mcqs.explanation: SIGCHLD is delivered to a parent whenever a child exits or stops, so it knows to call wait() and reap it. SIGCONT resumes a stopped process, SIGTERM asks a process to terminate, and SIGINT is the Ctrl+C interrupt — none of them relate to child-exit notification.

mcqs.question: Why can't a process install a handler for SIGKILL the way it can for SIGTERM?
options: The kernel enforces SIGKILL's default action unconditionally, so the system always has a guaranteed way to terminate a process no matter what code it's running
SIGKILL is deprecated and kept only for backward compatibility
SIGKILL requires root privileges to catch, which most processes lack
SIGKILL is actually catchable, but doing so is considered bad practice
mcqs.explanation: SIGKILL and SIGSTOP are special-cased so termination and suspension always work, even against malicious or badly broken code that swallows every catchable signal. It isn't deprecated, isn't gated on privilege, and genuinely cannot be caught by any process.

mcqs.question: Why is calling malloc() inside a signal handler dangerous?
options: malloc() is too slow to run inside a handler and will miss the delivery deadline
malloc() only works in multi-threaded programs, not single-threaded ones
If the handler interrupts code already inside malloc() with its internal lock held, the handler's own malloc() call can deadlock or corrupt the heap
malloc() silently returns NULL whenever called from a handler
mcqs.explanation: malloc()'s non-reentrancy is the core issue: if a handler interrupts the main program mid-allocation and calls malloc() itself, the shared heap structure or lock can be left inconsistent. There's no signal-delivery deadline, no such threading restriction, and no guaranteed NULL return.

mcqs.question: Why do orchestrators send SIGTERM before SIGKILL when stopping a process, instead of going straight to SIGKILL?
options: SIGKILL doesn't exist on some Linux distributions
SIGTERM is faster to deliver than SIGKILL
SIGKILL only works on root-owned processes
SIGTERM gives the process a chance to close connections and flush state before dying; SIGKILL gives it none
mcqs.explanation: SIGTERM is catchable, letting a well-behaved process shut down cleanly; SIGKILL tears the process down unconditionally with zero cleanup. SIGKILL exists everywhere on Linux, delivery speed isn't the distinguishing factor, and neither signal is restricted to root-owned targets.

mcqs.question: A Kubernetes pod's terminationGracePeriodSeconds is set to 30. The container ignores SIGTERM and is still running after 30 seconds. What happens next?
options: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM again and waits another 30 seconds
Kubernetes sends SIGKILL, forcibly terminating the container mid-request if necessary
Kubernetes marks the pod as permanently stuck and takes no further action
The grace period automatically extends to give the process more time
mcqs.explanation: Once the grace period expires, Kubernetes escalates straight to SIGKILL — which can't be caught or ignored — to guarantee the container actually stops. It doesn't resend SIGTERM, doesn't auto-extend the timer, and doesn't leave the pod stuck.

mcqs.question: A handler logs a message with printf() and frees a buffer with free() before returning. What's the real risk, even though it looks simple?
options: printf() and free() are both slow, causing the handler to miss re-delivery of the same signal
Neither function is async-signal-safe; if the handler interrupts the main program already inside one of them, shared internal state can be corrupted
printf() cannot be linked into a program that also uses signal handlers
free() will always crash immediately when called from a handler
mcqs.explanation: The danger is reentrancy, not raw speed: both functions maintain internal, non-reentrant state (buffers, heap locks) that a handler can corrupt if it interrupts the same function mid-execution on the main thread. There's no such linking restriction, no guaranteed crash, and no re-delivery deadline being missed.
